name: BPC-157

lead: BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide modelled on a protein fragment from human gastric juice. Lifters use it hoping to heal tendons, ligaments, muscle and gut faster, so they can keep training and build physique.

Preclinical work suggests it may influence angiogenesis, growth-hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts and nitric oxide pathways, which could speed cell migration and repair. The literature is overwhelmingly rodent studies, largely from one research group, and a 2025 systematic review found almost no human clinical data.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide or through compounding channels and is often stacked with TB-500 in recovery routines. People use it around injuries for weeks.

Human safety data are minimal, so the risk profile is largely unknown. Concerns include product purity and identity, injection-site problems, and a theoretical concern that pro-angiogenic activity could matter for people with cancer risk. It has no approved medical use, US regulators have flagged evidence and safety gaps, and WADA prohibits it for tested athletes.

angle.text: BPC-157 is used by lifters who want faster healing of tendons and muscles so injuries cost less training time. Quicker repair means more consistent training and more muscle. Nearly all evidence is from animal studies, with very limited human data.

lead: BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound 157, also called bepecin or PL 14736) is a synthetic peptide of fifteen amino acids whose sequence is derived from a protein found in human gastric juice. It was developed from work by the pharmacologist Predrag Sikiric and colleagues at the University of Zagreb, who published on the parent peptide in 1993, and nearly all of the published research on it comes from animal experiments, a large share of them from that group [1][2][3].

In fitness, injury-recovery and looksmaxxing circles it is used as a recovery aid. The chain people describe runs from faster tendon, ligament, muscle and gut repair, to fewer missed training weeks and quicker return from surgery, to more consistent training and a better physique. Some looksmaxxing posts go further and propose it for skin or even facial-structure goals, ideas that rest on extrapolation from lab work rather than on any facial study [4][5][6][7]. It is usually obtained as a research peptide, from compounding pharmacies or from clinics, and is most often discussed alongside the thymosin beta-4 fragment TB-500 as a so-called wolverine stack [8][3].

No drug regulator has approved BPC-157 for human use. Published reviews describe the human data as small: a handful of pilot or retrospective studies and one phase 1 registration whose results were not submitted, against a preclinical literature of several hundred papers [1][9][10]. Its status has been changing quickly. Wikipedia reports that on 30 October 2026 the US Health Secretary announced it, with several other peptides, could be supplied by compounding pharmacies, while stating that this does not make it an approved drug [1].

paras: BPC-157 is a linear peptide with the sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val. It is described as a fragment of a larger gastric protein and is unusually stable, remaining intact in human gastric juice for more than 24 hours in the account given by Wikipedia [1]. In rodent models it has been reported to be active after intramuscular, intravenous, oral, intraperitoneal and topical administration [1][11].
A urine test based on weak cation exchange solid-phase extraction has been described, and the peptide was reported to be stable in urine for four days [1].

Wikipedia gives its formula as C62H98N16O22 and notes earlier code names including PL 10, PLD-116 and PL 14736, the last from the Croatian company Pliva, which investigated it in inflammatory bowel disease [1]. It is a short, proline-rich chain, a feature associated with its stability, and it is sold as a lyophilised powder or as oral and topical preparations [1][11].

Sikiric, a professor of pharmacology at Zagreb, built his work on the idea that gastric juice contains protective factors that defend the gut and other organs. A 1993 overview in the Journal of Physiology (Paris) described a gastric-juice peptide called BPC and what he called the stomach-stress-organoprotection hypothesis [2]. In 1994 the 15-amino-acid fragment BPC 157 was reported to protect rats against stress-, cysteamine- and ethanol-induced gastric and duodenal lesions, in a comparison with H2 receptor antagonists and other agents [12]. STAT News dates the first study to 1992 and says he has published well over 150 papers on the peptide [3].

Through the 1990s and 2000s the group published on its relation to the nitric oxide system, on counteracting NSAID toxicity, on colitis and on wound healing in rats [11][13][14][15]. Pliva trialled a version for inflammatory bowel disease, according to Wikipedia [1]. Interest in tendon repair came with later work, among them a 2011 study of tendon fibroblast outgrowth and migration [16], a 2014 study on growth hormone receptor expression [17] and a 2017 study linking it to VEGFR2 activation [18]. Reviews note that for two decades only a handful of groups published in depth [19].

STAT News reports that bodybuilders and gym-goers began using the peptide around 2010, with early supply from Chinese laboratories followed by UK and US sellers marketing it as a research chemical; by about 2018 peptide discussion had spread to Reddit, and it later reached mainstream wellness culture through podcasts, clinics and the Make America Healthy Again movement [3]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, similarly credits 2025 and 2026 social-media trends and endorsements for a surge of interest [8].

BPC-157 is not marketed for cosmetic purposes in the way topical products are. In appearance and training communities it is discussed as a way to speed recovery from tendon, ligament, muscle and joint injuries, so that training can continue, and some users also report it for gut complaints and, anecdotally, for conditions such as tinnitus [4][5][20][21][22].
Orthopaedic reviews note that clinicians and athletes increasingly use it despite its lack of approval and its prohibition in professional sport [9].

There are no approved medical uses. Wikipedia notes it has been used in functional medicine without regulatory approval, and that some jurisdictions have restricted it as a prescription-only medicine even though it is not available through legitimate prescription [1].

Laboratory work attributes several actions to BPC-157. In cell and chick-membrane assays it increased vessel density and activated VEGFR2, supporting a pro-angiogenic role [18]. In cultured tendon fibroblasts it raised growth hormone receptor expression [17] and promoted outgrowth, survival and migration of tendon cells [16]. A 2025 narrative review summarises the proposed pathways as VEGFR2 signalling, nitric oxide synthesis through Akt-eNOS, and ERK1/2 signalling, with anti-inflammatory effects [10].

Sikiric's group has long described an interaction with the nitric oxide system, reporting that BPC 157 counteracted lesions produced by NOS inhibition in rats [11][2]. These mechanistic claims come from preclinical work and have not been confirmed in controlled human studies [19][10].

Wikipedia states BPC-157 is bioavailable in rodent models when given intramuscularly or intravenously [1]. A 2025 systematic review in an orthopaedic journal set out to cover metabolism and safety alongside mechanism, but human pharmacokinetic data are sparse [9].

Reviews of the animal literature describe consistent positive findings. A 2019 review of musculoskeletal studies reported prompt healing across tendon, ligament and muscle injury models, while stressing that most work used small rodent models, that only a handful of research groups had published in depth, and that efficacy in humans was not yet confirmed [19]. A 2018 review concluded that BPC 157 was consistently effective across a range of gastrointestinal injury models in animals when given alone [11]. A 2021 review covers rat skin wounds, burns and diabetic ulcers [13].

Individual studies include an alkali-burn wound model in rats where topical treatment accelerated wound closure [23], and early work from 1994 comparing it with H2 receptor antagonists in rat gastric and duodenal lesion models [12].

In humans, the evidence base is much smaller. A 2025 scoping review identified only three pilot studies in people, covering intra-articular knee pain, interstitial cystitis and intravenous administration [10]. Wikipedia describes a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain and a phase 1 trial in healthy volunteers whose results were not submitted [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports similar small studies including a 16-patient knee retrospective review and a 12-patient interstitial cystitis study [8]. Reviewers consistently describe the human evidence as too limited to establish efficacy [24][9][10].

Animal reports cover a wide range. The group and its collaborators describe benefit in rat models of colitis and ischaemia and reperfusion injury [25], in NSAID-induced gut damage [14], and in tendon, ligament, muscle and bone healing [11][19]. Reviewers note, as the main limitation, that the work is concentrated in a small number of laboratories and that independent replication in larger animals and in people is limited [19][9][3].

Controlled human trials are scarce. A 2025 systematic review in the HSS Journal searched the literature to June 2024, identified 544 articles and included 36; 35 were preclinical and one was clinical, a retrospective review of 12 patients with chronic knee pain, of whom seven reported relief lasting over six months. The authors concluded that BPC-157 may help musculoskeletal recovery based on level IV and V evidence, and noted that no clinical safety data were found [9][26].

The knee study itself (Lee and Padgett, 2021) was a retrospective chart review at a Florida clinic covering 2019 to 2020. Patients who had received intra-articular BPC-157, in four cases with thymosin beta-4, were surveyed by phone months later; 14 of the 16 reached reported pain relief. There was no control group and no validated outcome measures, and the authors themselves describe the study as small [26]. A 2024 pilot by Lee and colleagues treated 12 women with interstitial cystitis who had not responded to a standard drug, using BPC-157 delivered to the bladder wall during cystoscopy; all rated the global response 5 out of 5 and none reported adverse events, again without a control group [26]. A 2025 scoping review counts these and a small intravenous safety report as the only three human pilot studies, calls for large rigorous trials and advises that the compound be treated as investigational [10][26].

Several trials are registered. A phase 1 trial of BPC-157 for recovery after rotator cuff repair (NCT07803250, planned n=30) was listed as not yet recruiting, with a start date in 2027 [27]. A phase 2 trial for acute hamstring muscle strain (NCT07437547, n=120) was listed as recruiting from February 2026 [28]. A phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetics registration in healthy volunteers (NCT02637284, n=42) has an unknown status [29]. STAT News reports that Sikiric's group has described a 2015 Tijuana trial of an oral form as showing safety, but that its data were withdrawn from ClinicalTrials.gov and no results were provided; STAT also reports undisclosed corporate ties of the researcher, which he has not commented on [3]. A small completed trial of peptide gummies on inflammation and post-exercise recovery (NCT07752381, n=40) has also been registered; results have not been published [30]. Registrations are not results.

A 2025 patent and literature review states that few side effects have been reported and describes a favourable safety profile in animals, while also noting that the lack of comprehensive human studies is why regulators have not approved it [24]. A 2021 review notes no reported toxicity in the animal work (an LD1 was not reached) [13].

Wikipedia notes a theoretical concern: because the compound promotes angiogenesis, it might promote cancer or enlarge undetected cancers [1]. A 2025 narrative review of musculoskeletal use similarly lists safety concerns alongside regenerative potential and notes that human data are extremely limited [10]. Health authorities discourage use because human safety data are insufficient [1].
Products sold as research peptides are unregulated; questions about purity, identity and contamination apply, as raised in general reviews of gray-market injectable peptides.

STAT News reports that some users have described itching, severe anxiety and loss of pleasure after use, though causation is unclear, and that Matthew Fedoruk of the US Anti-Doping Agency has warned that buyers of unregulated product cannot know what is in the vial [3]. A Polish review group quoted by STAT raised the concern that new blood vessels could help tumours grow and noted that most studies come from Sikiric or a close colleague; Sikiric and colleagues dispute claims of harm, including cancer risk [3]. The HSS systematic review adds that adverse effects are possible because of unregulated manufacturing and contamination [9][26].

BPC-157 is not approved by any drug regulatory agency. Wikipedia states it is controlled as a prescription medicine in jurisdictions such as New Zealand and Australia despite not actually being available by prescription [1].

In sport, Wikipedia reports it has been banned by WADA since 2022 under the S0 category of non-exempt substances [1]. A 2025 review puts it differently, stating that it was temporarily banned in 2022 and is not currently listed [24]; sources therefore differ and the status may change.

Wikipedia reports that on 30 October 2026 the US Health Secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., announced that BPC-157, TB-500, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c and semax would be permitted to be supplied by compounding pharmacies despite lack of FDA approval [1]. Grokipedia, which is AI-generated and may contain errors, describes the policy as enforcement discretion for State-licensed pharmacies and licensed physicians under section 503A, with conditions such as a certificate of analysis, single-ingredient products, adverse-event reporting and a patient-specific prescription, and states it does not make BPC-157 an approved drug. Grokipedia also reports earlier steps, including a Category 2 bulk-substance classification in 2023 and an advisory committee vote in 2026 [8].

STAT News reports that the FDA treats BPC-157 as an unapproved drug, placed it among substances it advised should not be compounded in 2023 over concerns about immune response, impurities and incomplete safety data, and has issued warning letters to illegal sellers while enforcement has been limited [3]. Grokipedia says an FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 6 in July 2026 to recommend adding it to the 503A bulk substances list, a non-binding step [8]. The Australian TGA and New Zealand's Medsafe have also addressed peptides in recent scheduling notices, according to Wikipedia [1].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: On the T Nation forum, BPC-157 appears frequently in training logs and injury threads. Users describe injecting it near an injured joint or muscle, and pair it with TB-500 [4][5][20]. Posters say it helped with tennis elbow, muscle tears or post-surgical recovery [5][20][21]. Others describe it more cautiously: one poster calls it a lubricant that helps promote healing and notes it is nothing like growth hormone [31], and another says its strength is not inflammation [4].

Vendors typically label the product for research purposes only, and forum users refer to purchasing it on that basis [20]. Grokipedia reports a surge in popularity during 2025 and 2026 driven by social media and public figures, which is an unverified claim from an AI-generated source [8].

STAT News names several promoters: a Florida endocrinologist, Edwin Lee, who prescribes it through a compounding pharmacy and co-founded a peptide advocacy group; the wellness entrepreneur Gary Brecka, who sells BPC-157 sprays and patches; and podcast guests on shows hosted by Andrew Huberman and Joe Rogan who have praised it [3]. Users speak of the combination of BPC-157 and TB-500 as the wolverine stack; TB-500 is a synthetic version of part of thymosin beta-4, a protein that WADA also bans in sport and that was central to doping cases in Australian rugby league and football in the 2010s [32][8].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing communities beyond recovery
paras: On looksmax.org, German-language and English threads ask about running BPC-157 with TB-500 for gym injuries and post-surgery recovery, and one user says they used both around surgery and after a training injury [33]. Another thread asks, in the context of a teenage poster's looks goals, whether oral BPC-157 would close growth plates; replies tell the poster they do not need it [34]. A third, framed as a guide, proposes that BPC-157 and TB-500 could remodel facial bone sutures and widen the cheekbones, citing orthopaedic research on tissue repair and the poster's own measurements; a reply in the thread suggests the post was generated by an AI tool [6]. No published study has examined BPC-157 for facial bone structure. Other threads discuss pairing it with the copper peptide GHK-Cu for skin [7].

Ongoing registrations in rotator cuff repair and hamstring strain suggest the first controlled human trials in sports-injury settings [27][28]. Reviewers call for well-designed clinical trials and independent replication outside the original research group before conclusions about efficacy in humans can be drawn [19][9][10].

TB-500 is the usual companion in forum protocols and is a synthetic form of an active region of thymosin beta-4, a peptide that Wikipedia says was sequenced in 1981 and that has been tested in phase 2 trials of skin ulcers and eye conditions [32]. GHK-Cu, KPV, MOTS-c, epitalon and semax are other peptides named alongside BPC-157 in the October 2026 US compounding announcement and in community discussion [1][7].

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar fitness forums, BPC-157 is one of the most commonly mentioned recovery peptides, usually discussed alongside TB-500 for injuries and surgery recovery. [4][5]

claims.claim: BPC-157 heals tendon and muscle injuries much faster than normal.
BPC-157 and TB-500 work synergistically as a 'recovery stack'.
It is safe because there are almost no reported side effects.
BPC-157 helps with other problems such as tinnitus or gut conditions.
Doctors do not prescribe it because it 'makes you better' and is not profitable.
BPC-157 can remodel facial bones and widen cheekbones when stacked with TB-500.
BPC-157 is natural and therefore safe.
The wolverine stack is for more than injuries and works for gut, skin and brain problems.

timeline.event: Sikiric's group at the University of Zagreb publishes on a gastric-juice peptide, BPC (STAT dates the first study to 1992; the 1993 overview is in the Journal of Physiology, Paris). [2][3]
The 15-amino-acid fragment BPC 157 is reported to protect against experimental gastric and duodenal lesions in rats. [12]
Bodybuilders begin using the peptide, initially from Chinese laboratories; 2011 study reports promotion of tendon fibroblast outgrowth, survival and migration. [16][3]
BPC 157 is reported to raise growth hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts. [17]
A study links BPC 157 to VEGFR2 activation and angiogenesis. [18]
Peptide discussion, including BPC-157, spreads on Reddit. [3]
Retrospective report of intra-articular BPC-157 for knee pain in 16 contacted patients is published. [26]
WADA prohibition is reported by Wikipedia; a 2025 review describes it as temporary. [1][24]
The FDA places BPC-157 among substances not to be compounded, citing immunogenicity, impurity and safety-data concerns. [8][3]
Pilot report of BPC-157 for interstitial cystitis in 12 women. [26]
Systematic and scoping reviews find very limited human data. [9][10]
STAT News profiles the peptide's rise from gym use to wellness culture. [3]
An FDA advisory committee votes 8 to 6 in favour of recommending it for the 503A bulk substances list, per Grokipedia. [8]
HHS announces enforcement discretion allowing compounding of BPC-157 and five other peptides, per Wikipedia. [1]
